(Commentary)
Here's the thing about all the agita related to the Los Angeles Dodgers, MLB's competitive balance and the 2026 postseason: No outcome this October will change the calculus for the team owners.
Even if the small-market Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians win the World Series, the league will continue its push for a salary cap, contending the sport lacks sufficient parity and is effectively broken.
Not that long ago, the league was making precisely the opposite argument. Its public-relations department, in news releases before the 2021 and 2022 seasons, described competitive balance as a hallmark of MLB.
Let's be clear: Revenue disparity between large- and small-market clubs is a legitimate concern. The league and players union need to adopt significant measures to make the playing field more level. But the league's argument for greater competitive balance, if not a red herring, is at least an argument of convenience. And not a particularly strong one, if you watched the regular season.
The Brewers finished with the best record in the National League. The Rays produced the best record in the American League. And the Guardians became the third small-market team to earn one of four first-round byes. Perhaps the Guardians were undeserving, considering their record was only the 11th best in the majors. But by finishing with the second-best mark among AL division winners, they clinched the bye under the postseason format the league and union created.
So is the sport really that far gone?
The league's own news release in 2022 noted that MLB produced 15 different World Series champions in the prior 21 seasons. The Texas Rangers in 2023 made it 16. And before the 2024 World Series, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred told The Athletic, "Our record on competitive balance is darn good."
Just two years later, to hear Manfred & Co. tell it, the sport is having an existential crisis. All because the league's highest-revenue team, the Dodgers, won back-to-back World Series. All because the team owners want to build their case for a cap.
The league cites a need for greater competitive balance as justification to drastically overhaul the game's economic system. And it is trumpeting a new set of facts -- specifically, the absence of a small-market champion since the 2015 Kansas City Royals -- to make its case.
There is no denying that in that time, large-market teams have accounted for 90% of World Series winners, 85% of World Series participants and 77.5% of league championship series participants. And sure, the same pattern might continue this year.
Never mind that the Dodgers performed below expectations in the regular season for the second consecutive year. According to FanGraphs, they still stand the best chance of winning the World Series -- 36.7%, with the Brewers next at 11.6%. As if on cue, and in some cases by design, the Dodgers' best players are getting healthy and rounding into form.
If Los Angeles becomes the first team since the 1998 to 2000 New York Yankees to win three consecutive World Series titles, the league will surely use that data point in its pitch that only a salary cap can save the sport.
And if the Brewers or Rays win their first Series, or if the Guardians win their first since 1948? The league will consider it an aberration, a single-season outcome that means little when compared with the larger sample size of the previous 10 seasons. An exception that proves the rule.
But let's broaden the discussion.
By emphasizing postseason results, the league is devaluing the most accurate measure of a club, the six-month grind of the regular season. Not to mention devaluing the 162 games of inventory all 30 clubs must sell.
Since 2015 -- the line of demarcation the league has set with the Royals' World Series triumph -- the Guardians rank fourth in regular-season wins, the Brewers fifth and the Rays seventh. They are models for other small-market teams, proof that those clubs do not have to operate without hope.
It's true none of those teams won a World Series in the past 10 years. But the Rays got there in the shortened 2020 season. The Guardians reached the American League Championship Series in 2024, the Brewers in 2025. Inferior depth, resulting in part from lower payrolls, might be part of the reason none went further. Adjustments to the collective bargaining agreement could help address that.
No reasonable person would start a league from scratch and adopt baseball's current economic system, in which the league says that the top four spenders -- the Dodgers, New York Mets, Yankees and Philadelphia Phillies -- outspent the bottom 22 in free agency over the course of the current labor agreement.
Reasonable people can disagree, however, whether a cap is the only possible solution when the players' historic opposition to the concept might lead to the cancellation of part or all of the 2027 season.
The league keeps referencing polls saying fans want a cap. Fans, though, evidently are not too upset with the current state of affairs: The league's attendance increased again this year, reaching its highest level since 2016.
Even in cap sports, not every team begins every season with the expectation of competing for a title. The most successful franchises are the shrewdest. Part of baseball's problem is that innovative small-market clubs no longer hold the competitive advantage they once did over less forward-thinking opponents.
Ex // Top Stories
Some of the large-market teams plucked top small-market executives. Very few clubs, if any, continue to lag behind in the intellectual arms race. Even the Colorado Rockies and Washington Nationals, two of the slowest clubs to adapt to baseball's information age, have gotten smarter.
If everyone is essentially working off the same data, payrolls become more of a separator. But even then, the edge money provides is not an absolute guarantee of success in October.
Before winning in the shortened 2020 season, the Dodgers had not won a World Series since 1988. The Mets have not won since 1986. The Phillies and Yankees are experiencing championship droughts that began in 2008 and 2009.
Many baseball executives consider the postseason a crapshoot, fearing the random outcomes that occur in small samples.
The Dodgers, without question, have inordinate financial advantages, including the right to withhold a healthy portion of their massive local TV deal from revenue sharing, a benefit that arose from a settlement the league reached in bankruptcy court with the team's former owner Frank McCourt.
Still, the Dodgers in 2022 and 2023 were eliminated in the division series by rivals from smaller markets, the San Diego Padres and Arizona Diamondbacks. In 2024, the Dodgers' first year with Shohei Ohtani, they nearly lost to the Padres again in division series play. And if not for a series of fortuitous events, they would have lost the 2025 World Series to the Toronto Blue Jays.
Another thing lost in the discussion about the Dodgers' dominance is that villains are good for business. This is the third consecutive season the Dodgers led the majors in road attendance. Their spending forces other NL clubs to try to keep pace. The small-market Padres, in particular, are better for it.
Yet the ability to spend is sometimes a double-edged sword. Long-term contracts sometimes backfire. Seemingly capable of papering over any mistake by simply printing more money, the Dodgers roll merrily along even when free-agent additions such as Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott slump. But several of the Dodgers' biggest and most expensive stars are facing age-related decline. A number of other top-10 payroll clubs, including the Padres, are locked into the same kinds of players.
None of that means that the league and union should proceed as if all is well, assuming the game's cyclical nature will balance things out. The concerns of the small-market clubs must be addressed, and the union acknowledged as much in May with its initial proposals, some of which addressed revenue disparity.
The union proposed enhanced revenue sharing that included protections "to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering"; financial rewards for successful revenue-sharing recipients and draft-pick incentives for them to sign free agents and retain their own players on the verge of hitting the open market.
The league scoffed at the union proposals, as one might expect with the collective bargaining agreement months away from expiration and the parties holding completely different worldviews. Finding a middle ground will be tricky. At least to this point, large-market clubs are willing to share more revenue -- and yield their inherent financial advantages -- but only under a cap system that fixes their costs.
Teams like the Brewers, Rays and Guardians clearly do not require more money to win regular-season games. But the way they operate, frequently trading stars as they get closer to free agency, is far from fan-friendly. Brewers fans buying a Jacob Misiorowski jersey and Rays fans buying a Junior Caminero jersey know not to get too attached to those players. As one small-market executive says: "Championships are won with talent, continuity and experience. We can get talent. The other two are tough to come by."
Tough, but not impossible. Countless examples exist of revenue-sharing recipients signing homegrown players for the long term. The Brewers did it with Jackson Chourio, Cooper Pratt and Luis Lara, the Guardians with José Ramírez and Tanner Bibee. The Pittsburgh Pirates might not keep Paul Skenes, but they locked up Konnor Griffin. The Royals secured extensions with Bobby Witt Jr. and Maikel Garcia, the Seattle Mariners with Cal Raleigh and Julio Rodríguez, the Arizona Diamondbacks with Corbin Carroll and Geraldo Perdomo.
Based on its proposals, the union thinks giving small-market teams an even better opportunity to retain players would benefit the sport. A salary cap is not necessary to make those adjustments and others to the collective bargaining agreement. Much as the league would like fans to believe otherwise, this is not an all-or-nothing situation.
In June, a reporter asked Manfred why he portrays a league he described in 2024 as having a "darn good" record on competitive balance to be out of whack just two years later.
"In the context, particularly of the postseason, where you're trying to generate interest and maximize viewership, I think it's important to emphasize competitiveness," Manfred said. "And there are aspects of competitiveness."
He added: "When we think about it from a labor perspective, we're focused on an entirely different part of the calendar. And that's the offseason, when you're trying to sell season tickets, and the perception among our fans that's really strong that we have a lack of competitiveness."
Maximizing viewership in the postseason? Viewership in the United States last year was the sport's highest since 2017. Selling season tickets? Sure, it's a problem in markets where team owners do not adequately invest in their franchises. It should be less of a problem in places like Milwaukee, Tampa Bay and Cleveland, if we're just talking about the product.
Make the current system fairer, and those clubs will stand even better chances of reaching a postseason that the league expanded to 12 teams from 10 in 2022. Give those clubs enough cracks at the postseason, and eventually one or more will break through.
It could happen this year, if the Brewers, Rays or Guardians win the World Series. The system needs improvement, no doubt. But if competitive balance is the object, it's a lot closer than it appears.

ATLANTA -- When Walt Weiss sends Chris Sale to the mound for Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series on Tuesday afternoon, he’ll have the same confidence he possessed more than a quarter of a century ago, when he was playing behind John Smoltz, Tom Glavine and Greg Maddux in postseason games.
“There’s a different feeling when a guy like that is taking the mound,” Weiss said. “We felt it those years with the Big Three, and I felt it at other times in my career. I felt it in Oakland with Dave Stewart. I think it elevates the room the day that guy is pitching.”
Weiss made three straight trips to the playoffs as Atlanta’s shortstop from 1998-2000, and he’s experienced the postseason seven of the past eight years as the team’s bench coach. So, Braves playoff baseball is nothing new for him.
But, for Sale, this will be an experience he has long awaited.
The 37-year-old left-hander’s back prevented him from pitching in the postseason during his 2024 NL Cy Young Award season. But the splendid year he has produced during this third season with Atlanta will be enriched when he throws the first pitch of this Wild Card Series against the Phillies on Tuesday at 2 p.m. ET (NBC/Peacock).
“I love pitching here in Atlanta,” Sale said. “I love pitching in front of these fans, and being able to do it in the postseason makes it that much more special.”
Sale’s greatest postseason moment occurred when he concluded the 2018 World Series for the Red Sox by striking out each of the three batters he faced in the ninth inning of Game 5. His most recent playoff experience occurred in 2021, when, two months after returning from Tommy John surgery, he made three frustrating starts for Boston.
Five years later, Sale is in a far different position. After injuries limited him to a total of 151 innings from 2020-23, the Red Sox essentially gave up on him and sent him to Atlanta prior to the 2024 season. The lanky lefty flourished that year, and has continued to get better. The 2.16 ERA he produced this year ranked third in MLB, and it stands as the fifth-best mark produced by any Braves pitcher who has made at least 25 starts in any season going back to 1920.
So, there truly is reason to think this year’s postseason experience might be different. Sale has constructed a 7.24 ERA in seven previous playoff starts. His struggles weren’t restricted to the 2021 experience. He posted a 6.87 ERA in the four postseason starts he made in 2017 and ‘18. He allowed seven earned runs in one and lasted fewer than five innings in two others.
“I think you learn that it's just about harnessing the energy,” Sale said. “I learned this from David Tollett, my college coach [at Florida Gulf Coast University] -- you can't be better than you are. You can't play above what you possess, and sometimes you go out there and try to do too much, and actually do less.”
The opponents and pitching matchups Sale drew over the past two months prepared him for what he could encounter over the next few weeks. While posting a 2.36 ERA over his final seven starts, he pitched against four playoff teams (Yankees, Brewers, Dodgers and twice against the Phillies) and one (D-backs) that nearly made the postseason.
Within this same stretch, Sale matched up against top-flight starters Gerrit Cole, Jacob Misiorowski, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Cristopher Sánchez and Aaron Nola.
“He’s been nothing short of amazing for us,” Braves first baseman Matt Olson said. “I wouldn’t want anybody else taking the mound for us tomorrow.”
Sale certainly has reason to enter this assignment with confidence. He posted a 2.08 ERA in four starts against the Phillies this season, and the Braves won each of those contests.
If he can garner similar results on Tuesday, there’s a good chance this won’t be the only postseason start he will make this year.
“He presents a whole set of problems, but we've seen him a [few times],” Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. “We haven't been great with him, but we'll see. Tomorrow is a new day.”

SAN DIEGO — The Chicago Cubs are again turning to left-hander Matthew Boyd to begin their postseason.
Boyd, who got the Game 1 start in last year’s wild-card series against the San Diego Padres, will again get the ball when the Cubs open their rematch Tuesday, this time at Petco Park. The Cubs also could have started right-hander Kevin Gausman but opted for the lefty. Boyd held the Padres to one run in 4 1/3 innings in Game 1 last season at Wrigley Field.
“The first two months of the season were certainly interrupted and not smooth, but since then he’s gotten into a routine and consistency, that is what I think Matthew offers,” manager Craig Counsell said Monday after their team workout. “Playoff starts are a challenge. Matthew’s experienced in that and had good experiences last year with it for us and look for him to do the same tomorrow.”
Since returning from meniscus surgery June 25, Boyd posted a 3.42 ERA in his final 17 starts, allowing three earned runs or fewer in 12 of those outings.
Counsell didn’t provide specifics on who could start Games 2 or 3, the latter if necessary Thursday. Gausman is expected to pitch at some point in the series. His left shoulder injury sustained in his final regular-season start Wednesday created some uncertainty about whether he would be available this playoff round. The Cubs feel Gausman’s shoulder is trending well but isn’t fully in the clear, making a Tuesday start not a realistic option.
The Cubs are expected to carry 12 pitchers on their wild-card roster. Left-hander Shota Imanaga is also expected to factor into the Cubs’ pitching plans this series, though Counsell cautioned he didn’t know whether that would be as a starter or a reliever. Right-hander Clay Holmes wasn’t at his best down the stretch, but the Cubs anticipate him providing bulk in some capacity this series, whether that’s in a start or multiple innings out of the bullpen.
The best-of-three series allows Counsell to fully deploy all his pitchers as needed, whether it’s using starters out of the bullpen for multiple frames or even one-inning appearances. The Cubs will seek the best matchups and pockets of hitters for their pitchers to face.
“I look at these games kind of in this context that we’re talking about the urgency is you have 27 outs, we’ve got to figure out how to get 27 outs,” Counsell said. “The order that that happens — starter, reliever, closer, setup man — those words don’t matter. We’re just trying to get 27 outs.”
The Cubs’ pitching plans beyond Game 1 will be dictated by whether they win or lose the opener. It’ll be all hands on deck Wednesday for Game 2 if they don’t pull out the win Tuesday.
“It doesn’t matter how anything happens tomorrow, like aesthetically, it just matters that we win, that’s the bottom line,” Counsell said. “Because we’ve got to win two games in the next three days and so how anybody does, how anything happens, it doesn’t matter. You’ve got to win the game. And I think you probably lean more on the process over 162 games because you have to. But when you get to a two-out-of-three series to play the next game, your thoughts have to change a little bit.”
In a rematch of last year’s wild-card matchup, a venue change presents an added challenge for the Cubs against a Padres team with one of the best home records in baseball — 51-30 at Petco Park this year compared to 40-41 on the road.
The Cubs haven’t decided yet whether Alex Bregman is feeling well enough to start at third base or if they keep using him as the designated hitter to reduce the risk as he continues to play with multiple facial fractures. He took grounders at third base during live batting practice Monday, an encouraging development.
Bregman’s quick return gives the Cubs’ lineup added juice.
“I definitely think that fires you up,” Pete Crow-Armstrong said Monday. “Knowing him and how wonderfully crazed he is just about his work and how much he loves the game, not really surprising. Not to put a damper on how cool it is that he is coming back after eight facial fractures and whatnot, like, I’m just not surprised. He lives for this kind of baseball.”

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO — The playoffs have arrived.
The Cubs have been building to this all season long, eyeing a run deep into October.
‘‘This group is ready,’’ catcher Carson Kelly said Sunday. ‘‘It’s been a long year. We’ve had our ups and downs. But what this group does really well is we come prepared every single day.’’
To get to where they want to go, the Cubs first need to get past the Padres, their opponent in a best-of-three wild-card series.
Here’s what could make the difference:
Pete Crow-Armstrong
Crow-Armstrong has been the best player in baseball this season and soon will have an MVP award on his mantel to show for it.
But the individual accolades have meant little to Crow-Armstrong, given that he’s focused on team goals. The chase for the biggest of those — a World Series title — starts now.
It’s a team sport, and everyone will have to do their job for the Cubs to win. But if you’re going to talk about the impact one player can make, Crow-Armstrong can make more than just about anyone else in the playoffs.
‘‘We’re fortunate we get to see it in person every single day,’’ Kelly said. ‘‘There are a lot of times where we’ll look at each other and say, ‘Oh, my gosh, did that really just happen?’
‘‘Sometimes he gets up there, and you’re like, ‘OK, Pete’s going to hit a homer.’ He hits it, and you’re like, ‘What?’ Or running a ball down in the gap. Stealing a base, stealing second and third. You’re like, ‘This guy, he does it all.’ ’’
Alex Bregman
A week ago, the Cubs didn’t know what Bregman would be able to give them, if anything, in the postseason after taking a foul ball off his face.
But not only are they able to include Bregman in their playoff plans, they can count him as a
centerpiece.
A week removed from his freak injury, Bregman homered twice as part of a four-hit Sunday.
San Diego. Drink it in. It always goes down smooth. Just like these couple two tree things about the Cubs the night before the playoffs start. @suntimes_sports @Suntimes pic.twitter.com/2j45VXUP43
— Vinnie Duber (@VinnieDuber) September 29, 2026
Bregman got back to being Bregman in a hurry, and that’s a big deal. The Cubs signed him to a five-year, $175 million free-agent deal in part to be a force in October, where he’s one of the most accomplished postseason hitters of all time.
And showing some Chicago toughness helps, too.
‘‘It fires you up,’’ Crow-Armstrong said Monday. ‘‘Knowing him and how wonderfully crazed he is about his work and how much he loves the game, it’s not really surprising. Not to put a damper on how cool it is, him coming back after eight facial fractures and whatnot, I’m just not that surprised. He lives for this kind of baseball.
‘‘Most important, I’m glad he’s healthy enough to do what he loves. But selfishly, I’m pumped that he’s going to be in our lineup for these important games. Simply put, Alex Bregman makes our lineup better, so it’s huge he’s getting himself game-ready.’’
The bullpen
It wasn’t long ago that the Cubs’ bullpen was in disarray.
But things have stabilized a bit, with manager Craig Counsell leaning on right-handers Ryan Zeferjahn (1.13 ERA in his last nine outings) and Daniel Palencia (eight scoreless appearances in a row) to great effect.
Palencia is looking more like the guy who dazzled last season, and Zeferjahn is looking more like the guy the Cubs thought they landed in a deadline deal.
‘‘He’s had some good outings lately,’’ Counsell said of Zeferjahn. ‘‘I feel great about him. He’s going to pitch. He’s going to be a major part of this at the end here.’’
The Cubs don’t necessarily have a designated closer, not that they see that as a problem, given Counsell’s ‘‘out-getters’’ mantra. But should any fans fret that is the team’s Achilles’ heel, maybe Zeferjahn can put their minds at ease.
‘‘There’s ups and downs, and I rode that ‘down’ for a little bit,’’ Zeferjahn said. ‘‘But I’ve been working my way back up. . . . Hopefully, I’m riding an all-time high here going into the playoffs.’’
The conditions
The Cubs led baseball in runs scored this season, but the bats didn’t look great last week, averaging just two runs a game.
But heading to San Diego could have its advantages.
Kelly compared trying to hit at Wrigley Field and Fenway Park last week — they scored nine total runs in five games at the cold, windy venues — “like you’re hitting into a fan.”
The Cubs moved indoors Sunday and scored six runs. That’s only one game, hardly an indicator of what’s to come. But not dealing with poor hitting conditions is one way to allow a capable Cubs lineup to flex its muscles.
The catch? They might have to get real muscly, as the Padres — quite used to hitting in nice weather — have been on a roll, with only one team in baseball (the Brewers) scoring more runs in September.

On Sunday, the Atlanta Braves finished their final game of the 2026 regular season when they lost to the Miami Marlins (in Florida) by a score of 5-3.
The Braves will now open up a playoff series with Bryce Harper and the Philadelphia Phillies on Tuesday afternoon at Truist Park.
Riley’s Wife Sends Out Heartfelt IG Post
Earlier this month, news came out that Austin Riley was nominated for the 2026 Roberto Clemente Award.
Atlanta Braves Foundation wrote (on September 14): “For all his efforts to give back to Braves Country, Austin Riley has been named the Braves nominee for the 2026 Roberto Clemente Award!”
Riley’s wife (Anna) sent out a heartfelt post for Riley earlier this week.
She wrote (in a joint post with Austin): “so proud of all the work you do on & off the field!!!”
Here’s what people were saying in the comments:
Brewer Hicklen: “Congrats man! Well deserved!”
@kenzieheim: “The most perfect fam!!! Cheering for yall! ❤️❤️”
@ambermaebum: “Congratulations Riley Fam ❤️”
@jamie_alt_lane: “Braves Country is proud of you!”
@susan_rodgers48: “Congratulations Austin you’re amazing and have such a beautiful family!⚾️🪓👏🏻👏🏻👏🏻👏🏻”
@tarawooley: “Beautiful family! Congratulations!! 🎉💞😊 Such a well-deserved honor and accomplishment!”
Looking At Riley
Riley was picked in the 1st round of the 2015 MLB Draft.
He is in the middle of his 8th season at the MLB level (all with the Braves).
The two-time MLB All-Star finished the regular season batting .219 with 124 hits, 19 home runs, 72 RBIs, 64 runs and nine stolen bases in 159 games.
Looking At The Braves Right Now
The Braves finished the regular season with a 94-68 record.
They won the National League East division title.
After missing the 2025 MLB playoffs, the Braves look like a true contender to win the World Series this year.

On Monday, the Philadelphia Phillies are off following Sunday’s 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays.
With the victory, they clinched a spot in the 2026 MLB playoffs.
The Phillies will now go to Atlanta for a three-game series with the Braves at Truist Park (starting on Tuesday).
Bryce Harper Makes Honest Statement
Bryce Harper has had many battles with the Braves over his career.
Ahead of the series, he met with the media.
Harper (via Chad Bishop of AJC): “I love playing here. This is one of my favorite parks to play in. I love the field. I love the setup of it. I enjoy coming into Atlanta and playing. Obviously, the crowd’s in it. They love their team. And it’s just a lot of fun coming in here and playing.”
Social Media Reacts To Harper Comments
Here’s what people were saying in the comments of Bishop’s post:
@calfenn_: “Man I wish we somehow had signed him. Would have been a great 1/2 with Acuña”
@JeninATL: “Stop making me like him!”
@gpphipps10: “He’s a great guy. Just hate him being a Philly”
@hjw2B: “I’d love being able to come down and play in Atlanta too if I had to spend most my time in Philly.”
@bravescarly3: “Hey Bryce, glad you like the city so much. How about tomorrow afternoon you explore the beltline and take your family to the aquarium. It will be a wonderful day out”
Looking At Harper
Harper is in the middle of his 8th season with the Phillies.
He led the franchise to the 2022 World Series.
Prior to Philadelphia, Harper had spent the first seven years of his career with the Washington Nationals.
The two-time MVP finished the 2026 regular season batting .269 with 29 home runs and 87 RBIs in 162 games.

ATLANTA — Yes, these Phillies.
The same core that has reached the postseason five consecutive years, yet hasn't won a playoff series since 2023, has another opportunity to finish what it started.
But Bryce Harper sees some differences in this version of the Phillies, even if many of the names are familiar.
"I think they're different, but they have a little bit of the same DNA," Harper said Monday at Truist Park. "We have a lot of the same and similar DNA that we've had the last couple years, with a sprinkle of a couple other guys."
Those additions, along with the growth of several returning players, could help determine whether Philadelphia's latest postseason appearance ends differently from its previous two.
The most obvious change is in the bullpen.
Over the last two postseasons, Phillies relievers have combined for a 6.82 ERA, a 1.65 WHIP and six home runs allowed in 30 1/3 innings. Their ERA jumps to 11.42 when pitching with a lead.
News
Those numbers help explain why Philadelphia hasn't advanced beyond the NLDS in either of its last two appearances.
This year's relief group looks considerably different. José Alvarado is the only remaining member of the Phillies' 2023 bullpen, and after posting a 5.86 ERA this season, he isn't expected to handle the most important late-inning assignments.
Instead, Philadelphia has Jhoan Duran at the back end, with Jonathan Bowlan, Alex McFarlane and Chase Shugart among the newer faces who could be asked to get the ball to their closer.
The Phillies haven't seen how this group will respond together in October. That uncertainty leaves them with questions, but at least they'll be trying to solve a familiar problem with a different group of pitchers.
The offense, meanwhile, has undergone fewer changes. Philadelphia still relies heavily on Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Trea Turner, with Alec Bohm and Bryson Stott providing much of the production behind them.
And that group has something to prove.
Of the 12 teams that played multiple postseason series across 2024 and 2025, the Phillies had the lowest batting average, the lowest average with runners in scoring position and the highest chase rate.
Too often, Philadelphia has struggled to put the ball in play when it has an opportunity to score. It was one of the reasons the club acquired Luis Arraez in August, but a left ankle sprain suffered during the final week of the regular season will keep him off the Wild Card roster.
That puts more responsibility on the returning hitters to sustain rallies against an Atlanta pitching staff that begins the series with Chris Sale and Tyler Mahle.
Bohm and Stott enter the postseason swinging the bat well, something Turner believes reflects the growth he's witnessed within the clubhouse this year.
"I think it was just kind of cool to see guys struggle at times and then pull themselves out of it at times," Turner said. "It didn't go as well as it could have gone for a lot of us."
He pointed specifically to Bohm, whose difficult start gave way to a productive final several months.
"He's been such a good player for a long time, and then this second half or the last two-thirds of the season, he's been really, really good for us," Turner said.
But the Phillies have also introduced a different kind of hitter into the lower part of their lineup.
Justin Crawford, who made his major league debut earlier this season, has given Philadelphia another player capable of reaching base, putting pressure on the defense and delivering in important situations.
From June 14 through the end of the regular season, Crawford hit .294, the 15th-highest average in baseball among players who appeared in at least 80 games during that span. He ranked third among rookies who met that qualification.
His production with runners in scoring position was even more striking.
Crawford hit .491 in those situations over that stretch, the highest average among 109 players who met the same games-played requirement. His 1.131 OPS with runners in scoring position ranked fifth.
He won't necessarily start every postseason game. Crawford shares center-field duties with Derek Hill, whose speed, defense and production against left-handed pitching give interim manager Don Mattingly another way to construct his lineup.
Hill has made quite an impression on Harper.
"He's just a professional, I would say. He's got a professional mindset," Harper said. "Obviously having his pops, coming from a big-league family, I think that helps a lot."
Harper went a step further when discussing Hill's arrival, which came in a June trade with the Chicago White Sox.
"I think it's one of the better moves Dave has made for our organization bringing him in," Harper said, referring to president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski.
His praise extended well beyond Hill's production. Harper singled out the way the outfielder prepares, backs up bases, looks for opportunities to advance and helps Philadelphia's younger players.
"He's a gamer. He plays the game the right way, and you need guys like that on your team," Harper said.
Hill is also part of a trio that has developed a close bond away from the field.
Along with Bryan De La Cruz and Edmundo Sosa, he belongs to "Team Blessed," a group built around their shared faith and a competitive batting-cage routine during games. All three have contributed in important moments throughout the season, frequently coming off the bench without the benefit of regular at-bats.
Harper mentioned Hill and De La Cruz specifically when asked what makes this club different from previous Phillies postseason teams. Both have given Philadelphia additional options against left-handed pitching, something it lacked earlier in the year.
And Harper believes players in those supporting roles can end up being the ones everyone remembers.
"It's funny to look back on a lot of postseasons in baseball history," Harper said. "Not many of the superstar players play to their ability."
Harper himself is a notable exception.
Among the 109 hitters in postseason history with at least 200 plate appearances, his .986 OPS ranks third, trailing only Carlos Beltrán and Albert Pujols. His .596 slugging percentage is fourth.
But his point wasn't about the stars who have delivered in October. It was about the players whose contributions nobody saw coming.
Consider Travis Ishikawa, a part-time first baseman who found himself playing left field for the 2014 San Francisco Giants. In Game 5 of the NLCS, Ishikawa hit a three-run, walk-off homer against the Cardinals to send San Francisco to the World Series.
That's the type of player Harper had in mind when discussing Philadelphia's reserves.
"You never know who the October hero is going to be," Harper said. "Then you get to the end and you're like, man, that guy had a great postseason and you might never hear from him again."
Hill, De La Cruz, Sosa and Crawford will have opportunities to write their own postseason stories. For some, it will be their first chance to experience an October environment that Harper knows well.
His advice is to avoid treating it as a different game.
"All the work that you put in during the season and all the work that you put in to get you to this point, all that doesn't matter," Harper said. "It's the same game that we've been playing. It just might get a little bit quicker or might speed up on you a little bit if you let it."
That doesn't mean the veteran slugger wants his younger teammates to ignore the occasion.
"If you can really try to just enjoy the moment, I don't know, you could go 0-for-4 tomorrow or you could go 0-for-5 tomorrow or you can go 3-for-4 with two homers and win a game," Harper said. "If you just really take in the moment, take in the opportunity, there's no greater feeling."
The Phillies have considerable postseason experience, but this season has tested them in ways their more recent teams haven't necessarily encountered.
They began 9-19, underwent a managerial change and spent much of the year rearranging their pitching staff because of injuries and inconsistent performances.
There are similarities to 2022, when Philadelphia also changed managers after a difficult start before making an improbable run to the World Series. That team didn't secure its postseason berth until Oct. 3 and entered the playoffs having gone 11-14 in September.
Turner wasn't part of that club. He joined the Phillies the following offseason, and much of what stood out to him about this year's team had less to do with the final results than the way his teammates responded to their own struggles.
He recalled a recent conversation about Schwarber, who was still working through issues with his swing during the final days of the regular season.
"He's hit 380 homers in his career, and one of the best hitters in the game, and he's just not satisfied," Turner said.
For Turner, that restlessness says something about the veteran players who have been together through several disappointing postseason exits.
"Just seeing guys kind of manage their situations and want to compete and want to get back out there and just loving the game, I think that was pretty cool from a team standpoint," he said.
It's a perspective that comes from watching the same players through different stages of their careers. As Harper acknowledged, they're getting older. Stott has grown into a more established hitter, Bohm's future in Philadelphia is uncertain, and the club has brought in new players to complement a core that has been trying to win a championship for years.
The Phillies have invested heavily in their starting rotation, traded for a closer last year they believe can handle the biggest innings and introduced players who could give their offense a different look. But much of their postseason success will still depend on familiar names producing in situations where they've struggled before.
Harper, now preparing for his ninth postseason in 15 major league seasons, understands how rare those opportunities can become.
He brought up Hall-of-Fame quarterback Dan Marino, who reached the Super Bowl early in his career but never returned, as an example of how little a player's previous success guarantees about what comes next.
The Phillies have reached October five straight years. That doesn't mean they'll keep getting chances.
"I'm very lucky," Harper said. "Obviously I haven't got to the point where I want to be or our team hasn't either, but just to be in these moments, just to be given the opportunity to be here, I'm so grateful for that. It motivates me to get to these points."
Philadelphia arrives in Atlanta with many of the same stars, some new faces and the experience of a regular season that nearly slipped away from it.
Harper knows what he wants this group to accomplish. But after all the postseason games he's played, he's learned there's no telling which teammate might deliver the moment that gets them there.
"It's a cool opportunity for a lot of guys that have never played here," he said. "You could end up being a hero after having just an absolute terrible year."

The end of the 2026 season has been a rocky road for the Chicago Cubs. September was one of two months that saw them post sub-.500 marks on the season with an 11-13 record. They finished exactly .500 in their last 10 games. They dropped two winnable games against the Red Sox and two winnable games against the Marlins. It felt like they might be limping into the Postseason even before star third baseman Alex Bregman took a foul ball to the face, resulting in multiple fractures and multiple missed games for one of the Cubs best hitters in the second half.
Oh, you thought that was the bad news? There’s more! While that string of bad luck alone would have (probably) played the Cubs out of hosting a Wild Card Series at the Friendly Confines of Wrigley Field, Mother Nature wanted to get in on the action too. A freak September nor’easter descended upon Boston in the waning days of the 2026 season and MLB’s “solution” to this was the following itinerary for the Chicago Cubs:
- Thursday, Sept. 24: Day game at Wrigley, fly to Boston
- Friday, Sept. 25: Doubleheader in Boston, fly to Tampa
- Saturday, Sept. 26: Impromptu off day in Florida!
- Sunday, Sept. 27: Play one game in Tropicana Field to finish the season for #reasons, fly to San Diego
- Monday, Sept. 28: Workout day for the Wild Card Series
- Tuesday, Sept. 29: Begin best of three Wild Card Series in San Diego. First pitch scheduled at 10PM Eastern Time
It’s not particularly becoming in baseball to complain about certain things. After all, both teams have the same weather, the same umpires, the same roster rules and restrictions. They don’t have the same talent, but they did that to themselves and frankly, any difference in injury risk is likely a result of player decisions and tradeoffs someone made along the way as well. But this isn’t so much complaining as observing that MLB has chosen to deal the Cubs an absolutely brutal hand en route to the Postseason, which will kick off for them in San Diego tomorrow.
The question is, how will they handle it? You don’t have to look further than Bregman for answers. Bregman DH’d against the Red Sox and while it took a few at bats to get his timing back, he eventually did this [VIDEO].
It’s obviously an incorrect inference to suggest that two swings of the bat can salvage a downturn that likely reflects a depleted bullpen pitching on fumes. That said, stranger things have happened in this season that saw the Cubs win 10 games in a row twice and lose 10 straight in another stretch. It feels like the deck is stacked against the Cubs, but this isn’t really a team that has thrown in the towel or given up at any sign of adversity this season.
This team lost Cade Horton, Justin Steele had a setback, Ben Brown emerged as a legit TOR starter before being lost for the season and they kept winning anyway. Pete Crow-Armstrong looked like he was struggling early, only to emerge as the first 40-40 man in franchise history and the likely NL MVP. Alex Bregman hitting home runs with a broken face might just be the 2026 iteration of the Cubs channeling the 2016 team’s “We Never Quit.”
There’s no such thing as an easy road to a championship. The Cubs road continues tomorrow at Petco Park, and I doubt they’ll let something as trivial as jet lag define their season.

LOS ANGELES — October can be a powerful stain remover.
How much of a disappointing regular season can be washed away by a productive postseason – or just a key contribution at a pivotal moment?
“Everything,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I think we’ve seen it with Kiké (Hernandez). I think we’ve seen it with other guys … Chris Taylor has done it. We’re about winning championships, so I think the media, the fan base, if you perform at the right time, all is forgotten.”
Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman agrees.
“Oh, for sure,” Friedman said. “Like if you said, Player X can have a down regular season as compared to his previous performance but a really good October – I couldn’t pick it across the board because then we wouldn’t get a bye. But with one-offs, I would absolutely take that.”
This is an expensive one-off. Neither Hernandez nor Taylor carried the weight of a four-year, $240 million contract before emerging as postseason heroes.
Kyle Tucker signed that contract with the Dodgers last winter with the second-highest annual average value in MLB history behind teammate Shohei Ohtani. Then he went out and had the worst season of his career. Across the board, his slash line of .233/.330/.385 and OPS of .715 were the lowest since he played just 22 major-league games with the Houston Astros in 2019. His home run total (17), RBIs (70) and total bases (208) were the lowest in his five full seasons in the majors.
It’s the kind of performance when tied to that salary that would have made Tucker the target of fan vitriol and constant negative coverage by the media in many other MLB cities. It’s the kind of mistake that has sunk front offices in the past. With the Dodgers, though, Tucker just receded into the background of another 100-win season.
“I don’t know,” Tucker said when asked if he realized how differently his season would have landed had he signed with another team. “If I signed somewhere else and had a great year, everything could have been a different situation so I don’t really think or worry about what could have been. I just worry about where I’m at.”
And Tucker maintains that $60 million price tag on his season never weighed on him.
“I just show up and try to do my job,” he said. “I don’t really think about what I’m getting paid or what anyone else is getting paid.
“I guess (he was subject to less scrutiny on the Dodgers’ star-filled roster). I just show up. I don’t worry about all the other stuff. I just show up and play for the Dodgers and try to win for us.”
With few exceptions, Tucker showed up with no outward signs of the struggle or disappointment he might have been experiencing over the course of a season that didn’t meet anyone’s expectations. His low-key nature left reporters probing for signs that Tucker was affected by his performance, turning post-game interviews into mental health checks filled with questions about how Tucker was handling the disappointment, what he felt was behind his dismal home-and-road splits, who he turned to for support or where he found signs of hope in the darkness of a sub-.230 batting average.
“I don’t know,” Tucker said, laughing at that suggestion and turning the questions back on the reporter. “‘I’m good. How are you doing?’”
On the field, Tucker has been doing much better – a positive sign for a redemptive postseason as the team begins preparations for a best-of-five National League Division Series against Atlanta or Philadelphia that will begin Saturday at Dodger Stadium.
September was by far Tucker’s best month of his first season with the Dodgers. He hit .262 with an .889 OPS and six home runs.
“My recent play is more what I expected from myself,” said Tucker, crediting work with the hitting coaches to stabilize and improve his swing path for the September success.
“I just feel like my swing path and my approach and everything is in a really good spot. I just try to keep that going every single day and not really steer away from it. Whatever works works and try to keep doing it,” he said.
“Just trying to keep my swing path in the zone early and long. I’ve just been able to maintain that for awhile now. It’s just been hit and miss throughout the year and I wasn’t able to find something consistent that works.”
Before he discovered that and had his most productive month, there were questions about whether Tucker might be platooned or even benched during the postseason. In late August, Roberts said he addressed that speculation head on with Tucker, telling him “I’m going to ride or die” with you.
“He’s not much for reaction, so I think that he processed it. I think he was pleased,” Roberts said.
“It’s been fun to watch Kyle build some confidence (in September). … You can see him just freed up a little bit. He’s been working hard this whole year, and he’s been in it. And I give him a lot of credit for continuing to persevere and (I) expect the best of him to be at the end of the season.”
If that season ends with a World Series championship, Tucker expects that to be all anyone remembers about his first season as a Dodger.
“I mean, that’s why we play, to try and win a World Series,” he said. “Obviously the fan base expects that out of us. We expect that out of ourselves too.
“If you win a World Series no one cares. As long as you win the last game of the year, that’s all that matters.”

item.content:encoded:
For the 14th straight year, the Dodgers are postseason-bound.
Winners of three of the past six World Series, the Dodgers are looking to continue their reign. The back-to-back defending champions are bidding for the Major Leagues' first three-peat since the Yankees won three straight titles from 1998-2000.
The Dodgers, the No. 2 seed in the National League, are just about at full strength now that the likes of Shohei Ohtani, Andy Pages and Roki Sasaki have returned from the injured list, but there are several other compelling storylines to follow before the postseason.
Here's what to watch as the NL West-champion Dodgers forge their path back to the Fall Classic:
What could the postseason roster look like?
The strength of the Dodgers' pitching staff is the rotation, so expect them to carry more starters than they need and get creative with using some of them in relief. Manager Dave Roberts indicated that the team may carry only 12 pitchers to make room for an additional position player on the bench in the NL Division Series.
It may be premature to pencil in Josue De Paula, as the organization’s top prospect has played in only 11 big league games. But the Dodgers liked what they saw, and he could be an impact lefty bat off the bench.
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
First baseman (1): Freddie Freeman
Second baseman (1): Tommy Edman
Shortstop (1): Mookie Betts
Third baseman (1): Max Muncy
Outfielders (3): Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker
Utility/bench (3): Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas, Josue De Paula, Hyeseong Kim
Two-way player (1): Shohei Ohtani
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow
Relievers (9): Edwin Díaz, Tanner Scott, Edgardo Henriquez, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Roki Sasaki, Kris Bubic, Brock Stewart
When does the postseason begin?
The NL Division Series begin on Saturday.
Who could be the Dodgers' NLDS opponent? 
The Dodgers won their 13th NL West title in the past 14 seasons and secured a first-round bye, so they will play the winner of the Wild Card Series between the Braves and the Phillies.
Against which teams do the Dodgers have home-field advantage?
The Dodgers have home-field advantage over every team in the postseason field except the Brewers, who finished the regular season with the best record in the Majors.
What will the postseason rotation look like?
Yamamoto, Skubal, Snell and Glasnow make up this year's Big Four. The rotation order is yet to be determined. One consideration is that Yamamoto is accustomed to starting on at least five days' rest, whereas the other three are comfortable starting on four days' rest. That makes Yamamoto likely to start Game 1 of the NLDS because he would be available for a potential Game 5 on his normal rest. 
What's the latest on Ohtani's status?
Ohtani was activated from the 15-day IL and hit in the Dodgers' final five games, going 5-for-21 (.238) with eight strikeouts and one walk. Roberts described the performance as Ohtani showing some rust and said the team does not have any health concerns with him. 
Which injured players could return?   
The Dodgers hope that Henriquez, who has emerged as an important leverage arm, can return for the postseason after his regular season came to a premature end due to lower back discomfort. He will face hitters during the bye week, and as long as he comes away feeling good, he will be activated for the NLDS.
Which roster spots may be up for grabs?
The final spot on the bench is far from set in stone. The Dodgers could carry De Paula, but Dalton Rushing, Alex Call and Hyeseong Kim are additional options. This decision could come down to whether they want to use that bench spot on a potential impact bat or someone who brings enhanced speed and/or defense to the table. If L.A. carries fewer than 13 pitchers, that would open an additional bench spot.
The bullpen should also have some openings. If Henriquez does not recover in time for the postseason, that opens an additional spot. Justin Wrobleski, Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan were starters for most of the season, but they will be relief options in the postseason. But Wrobleski was inconsistent in the second half, and the Dodgers have other left-handers who may be more reliable in leverage, such as Bubic.
Who will close out games?
Díaz was supposed to resolve the Dodgers' ninth-inning troubles, but he has only added to them in his first year in L.A. Since returning from the IL, he has looked much better, which could have him back in the mix to close out games. The Dodgers may be more likely to play the matchups instead of going with a set closer in the postseason. Based on regular-season performance, Scott and Henriquez are two of the top options to pitch in save situations. Perhaps Sasaki could reprise his postseason closer role if needed.

Back in July, we celebrated the All-Star Game by looking at which participants had the best chance of eventually earning induction into the Hall of Fame. The likes of Bryce Harper, Justin Verlander, and Mike Trout all were locks, and rightfully so.
But as the MLB playoffs prepare to kick off, Verlander and Trout are once again sitting at home. Harper and the Phillies survived a near-collapse to secure a Wild Card seed, and he’s one of many postseason participants who could — and in his case, should — find themselves in the Hall of Fame one day.
Besides the obvious counting stats, what makes a Hall of Famer? As we’ve previously noted, baseball fans have recently accepted 40 bWAR as the standard for a remarkable career. Immaculate Grid is to thank on that front, even if there are players who have cleared that mark but don’t feel like Hall of Famers. Astros shortstop Carlos Correa, who is injured but has a 47.1 bWAR, is a perfect example, and he didn’t crack our list.
Instead, let’s turn our attention to someone who may very well become the second unanimous electee when his time comes.
Honorable mention: The Shohei Ohtani tier
Barring any unprecedented rule changes, Hall of Fame candidates must have 10 full seasons worth of experience for eligibility. That means Shohei Ohtani would technically be ineligible if he retired tomorrow, so he won’t land in the “lock” tier.
But Ohtani has always been a unicorn, so him having his own category makes all too much sense. We can all agree that, at this time next year, Ohtani should be a lock on that list.
Not yet eligible, but…
These guys don’t get their own table, but we wanted to address their situations ahead of the playoffs.
- Aroldis Chapman, P, Boston Red Sox: Off the numbers alone, Chapman and his 402 saves (ninth all-time) likely warrant induction. However, he also served a 30-game suspension in 2016 for violating the league’s domestic violence policy. It’s difficult to envision him earning the 75 percent required for election. Recent voting trends don’t work in favor of those who have been suspended for performance-enhancing drugs (more on that soon) or off-field incidents.
- Cam Schlittler, SP, New York Yankees and Jacob Misirowski, SP, Milwaukee Brewers: We’re lumping these two together because both will be trending during the playoffs. Just because these two are likely to win their league’s respective Cy Young Awards doesn’t mean they’re guaranteed a spot in Cooperstown. Heck, we don’t even know if they’ll pitch long enough to appear on a ballot! But, you know how baseball fans are.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., 2B/RF, San Diego Padres: As things currently stand, Tatis has no chance of getting into the Hall of Fame. Voters have made it clear that those who serve PED-related suspensions, as Tatis did in 2022, aren’t welcome in Cooperstown unless they buy a ticket. That said, we’re including him here
- Tarik Skubal, SP, Los Angeles Dodgers: Skubal became the 23rd pitcher in MLB history to win multiple Cy Young Awards, which will appeal to voters who prefer the "dominant" peak. But we’d like to see at least two or three more years of him being at least above-average. He’s also only seven seasons in, so he has a lot of work left.
On pace to make it into Cooperstown
- Alex Bregman, Chicago Cubs - 48.9 bWAR
- Matt Olson, Atlanta Braves - 44.2 bWAR
- Yordan Alvarez, DH, Houston Astros - 30.5 bWAR
These three have team success, specifically at least one World Series ring, working in their favor. Alvarez is likely to win AL MVP, and the 29-year-old is young enough that clearing 40 bWAR shouldn’t be an issue so long as healthy.
Bregman turns 33 next March, and his bWAR is likely far greater than you’d have guessed. But is he truly on a Hall of Fame trajectory? He's nowhere close to 2,000 hits (1,411) or 300 home runs (237), both of which are vital numbers when playing the hot corner.
Consider, though, that Bregman has averaged 24 home runs, 84 RBIs, 32 doubles, and 4.6 bWAR over the last five years. He’s under contract through 2030, and exceeded all of those numbers (28 home runs, 93 RBIs, 33 doubles, and 5.8 bWAR) this season.
If Bregman were to continue averaging those numbers, he’d end the 2031 season with 333 home runs, roughly 2,200 hits, and 481 doubles. Oh, and his bWAR would be right around 72.0, so we imagine he’d be a first-ballot inductee.
Unfortunately for him and Olson, the possibility of a work stoppage could have a monumental impact on their final counting stats. Which leads us into…
Borderline veterans
- Giancarlo Stanton, New York Yankees - 47.0 bWAR
- Zack Wheeler, Philadelphia Phillies - 46.6 bWAR
- Gerrit Cole, SP, New York Yankees - 45.8 bWAR
- Christian Yelich, Milwaukee Brewers - 45.1 bWAR
- Xander Bogaerts, SS, San Diego Padres - 44.3 bWAR
- Max Fried, P, New York Yankees - 32.3 bWAR
- Kyle Schwarber, OF/DH, Philadelphia Phillies - 22.3 bWAR
Stanton and Schwarber’s cases are likely dependent on whether they surpass 500 home runs. The latter will enter next season at 385 homers, and he turns 34 in March. But the looming work stoppage could significantly affect his chances of reaching 400 anytime soon.
As for Stanton, multiple lower-body injuries limited him to three homers in 24 games. Although he has 466 career home runs, the 2017 NL MVP turns 37 in November and is a free agent after next year.
The only members of the 500-home run club who aren’t in the Hall of Fame are either ineligible or have ties to performance-enhancing drugs. It’d be pretty remarkable if Schwarber and Stanton both cleared the historic total yet fell short of Cooperstown.
Personally, Wheeler and Cole are probably the only ones who will have a legitimate Hall of Fame résumé when they become eligible. The rest of those guys are Hall of Very Good at best. Much like Skubal, we need two or three more elite seasons from Fried before we’d even consider voting for him.
Go ahead and make the Hall of Fame plaque
- Mookie Betts, Los Angeles Dodgers - 79.0 bWAR
- Freddie Freeman, Los Angeles Dodgers - 66.8 bWAR
- Paul Goldschmidt, New York Yankees - 65.1 bWAR
- Aaron Judge, New York Yankees - 64.2 bWAR
- Manny Machado, San Diego Padres - 63.3 bWAR
- Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves - 62.7 bWAR
- José Ramírez, Cleveland Guardians - 60.3 bWAR
- Bryce Harper, Philadelphia Phillies - 56.9 bWAR
- Jose Altuve, Houston Astros - 53.4 bWAR
Outside of Goldschmidt and Sale, none of these names are overly surprising. And no, the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal shouldn’t impact Altuve, especially not after Carlos Beltrán just entered the Hall of Fame.
Goldschmidt currently ranks 143rd on the all-time bWAR list, and only 31 men above him aren’t already enshrined. But of the 20 who are or were eligible, most came up short for PED or off-field reasons. The question then becomes whether he’s wearing a Diamondbacks or Cardinals cap, or if he opts for the blank hat.
Although Sale turns 38 next March, he has a lifetime 2.95 ERA and 2,779 strikeouts, putting him within range of reaching 3,000. There’s absolutely no reason why he shouldn’t be a first-ballot selection.
As for the rest? You know a Hall of Famer when you see one, and they more than meet the expectations.

The Toronto Blue Jays entered 2026 expecting their offence to help carry them to another postseason run. Instead, a lineup that had been central to the club’s World Series appearance a year earlier became one of its biggest weaknesses. Established stars endured dramatic downturns, useful role players were asked to carry larger workloads and injuries forced Toronto to lean on several inexperienced hitters.
Anyone who watched the Blue Jays in 2026 knows they were not a good offensive team. They scored the fewest runs in all of baseball (648), hit the fewest home runs (152), and ranked second-worst in team OPS (.691) ahead of only the Los Angeles Angels.
There were still a few encouraging performances. But for every one of those successes they Blue Jays had another two or three hitters who fell short of expectations. The grades below weigh each hitter’s production against his role, opportunity and expectations entering the season.
Grading every Blue Jays hitter from the 2026 season
Alejandro Kirk
- HR: 10
- RBI: 43
- AVG: .278
- OPS: .767
- wRC+: 114
Kirk didn’t look like himself to start the year, then missed several months with a thumb injury. He recaptured his All-Star form when he finally returned, however, and led the Blue Jays offensively for much of the second half.
Grade: B+
Andrés Giménez
- HR: 9
- RBI: 59
- AVG: .244
- OPS: .649
- wRC+: 81
Giménez is what he is at this point: a below-average hitter with a knack for coming through in the clutch. He still managed to accrue 2.8 fWAR on the strength of his stellar glovework at shortstop and contributions on the basepaths.
Grade: B-
Brandon Valenzuela
- HR: 9
- RBI: 24
- AVG: .226
- OPS: .688
- wRC+: 96
Valenzuela filled in admirably for Kirk while he was on the injured list during the first half of the season. He flashed legitimate power upside at the plate before going ice-cold after the All-Star break, exposing the current limitations of his offensive profile.
Grade: C
Brett Bateman
- HR: 2
- RBI: 11
- AVG: .329
- OPS: .826
- wRC+: 138
Bateman exceeded all expectations after being acquired for Kevin Gausman at the trade deadline. He injected some life into the lineup immediately upon arrival and has likely cemented himself as a marquee piece of the 2027 squad.
Grade: A+
Charles McAdoo
- HR: 3
- RBI: 14
- AVG: .258
- OPS: .694
- wRC+: 93
McAdoo largely held his own at the plate with the Blue Jays in 2026. His approach needs work, but his combination of power and speed is exciting. He should keep improving with additional reps against MLB pitching.
Grade: C+
Davis Schneider
- HR: 5
- RBI: 16
- AVG: .145
- OPS: .624
- wRC+: 84
Schneider was one of several surprise contributors who propelled the Blue Jays to the World Series in 2025. His production fell off a cliff this year, which led to multiple demotions to Triple-A Buffalo. He might be out of runway.
Grade: F
Ernie Clement
- HR: 9
- RBI: 48
- AVG: .259
- OPS: .649
- wRC+: 80
It was a tale of two seasons for Clement. He rode a strong first half to his first career All-Star appearance, then devolved into one of baseball’s worst hitters from August onward. He ended the year with the worst offensive numbers of his career.
Grade: C-
George Springer
- HR: 15
- RBI: 54
- AVG: .249
- OPS: .726
- wRC+: 105
Springer redeemed what was likely his final season with the Blue Jays with a strong second half. While he didn’t come anywhere near his 2025 numbers, he still put together a solid season. His contract was worth every penny.
Grade: B-
Jésus Sánchez
- HR: 8
- RBI: 35
- AVG: .254
- OPS: .713
- wRC+: 99
He makes the list because he was on the team for most of the year before being designated for assignment in September. He failed to turn his power potential into actual production, and the less that can be said about his defence, the better.
Grade: D
Josh Smith
- HR: 6
- RBI: 15
- AVG: .203
- OPS: .611
- wRC+: 75
Smith was a pleasant surprise down the stretch after coming over in the Adam Macko trade, hitting five of his six home runs after coming to Toronto. He should have an opportunity to compete for a bench spot on the 2027 squad.
Grade: B-
Kazuma Okamoto
- HR: 33
- RBI: 92
- AVG: .232
- OPS: .762
- wRC+: 113
The general consensus on Okamoto coming over from Japan was that he would hit for a high average with some power. He ended up being more of a three true outcome guy who led the team in home runs, RBI, and strikeouts by a wide margin.
Grade: B+
Myles Straw
- HR: 3
- RBI: 26
- AVG: .241
- OPS: .646
- wRC+: 83
Straw wound up getting far more plate appearances than anyone expected he would coming into the year. Unsurprisingly, he didn’t do much with those opportunities. His value is in his speed, excellent defensive play, and clubhouse presence.
Grade: C+
Nathan Lukes:
- HR: 10
- RBI: 41
- AVG: .277
- OPS: .725
- wRC+: 102
Lukes got off to an extremely rough start at the plate while managing a bout of vertigo, but eventually settled back into his usual form. He’s a league-average hitter who grinds out at-bats—a quintessentially glue guy in a deeper lineup.
Grade: B
Sean Keys
- HR: 2
- RBI: 9
- AVG: .197
- OPS: .570
- wRC+: 57
Assigning Keys a letter grade almost feels unfair given how little he played. Still, he flashed some power potential in his limited opportunities, albeit while appearing generally overmatched by major league pitching. He’s very much a work in progress.
Grade: C
Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
- HR: 9
- RBI: 57
- AVG: .260
- OPS: .688
- wRC+: 95
This might be the most disappointing season by a hitter in the 50-year history of the franchise. Coming off a historic postseason, Guerrero authored one of the most pathetic performances by a superstar in recent memory. That ridiculous quote didn’t help, either.
Grade: F

It’s never too late to make a statement. A trio of perennial All-Stars proved that point during the final week of the 2026 regular season. Pete Alonso and Nolan Arenado went on offensive tears, finishing on resounding high notes to earn the year’s last Player of the Week Awards, while Ronald Acuña Jr. received Play of the Week honors for his spectacular warning-track grab on Saturday against the Marlins.
New York seems to awaken something within the Polar Bear. After hitting his 300th career homer back at Citi Field on Sept. 15, Alonso needed just eight more games to notch No. 307 – a jaw-dropping 471 foot shot – in a two-homer performance at Yankee Stadium on Friday night. Over his last five games in Toronto and the Bronx, Alonso reached base in 11 of his 22 plate appearances, recording five homers, eight RBIs and eight runs scored. The effort earned the first baseman his second Player of the Week Award of the second half.
Even with the Orioles’ final game of the season cancelled due to inclement weather, Alonso outpaced Yordan Alvarez to lead the American League in homers (43) and RBIs (113). He previously led the National League in RBIs with the Mets in 2022 (131), making him the first player in Major League history to lead both leagues in RBIs. He also played in every one of his team’s games for a third consecutive season.
The D-backs couldn’t complete their bid for the third NL Wild Card spot, but their veteran third baseman did just about everything he could to will them there. A game after hitting a go-ahead grand slam against the Yankees on Sept. 21, he finished a triple shy of the cycle at Coors Field on Tuesday to commence the ninth Player of the Week campaign of his career. Over the Snakes’ final six games in Colorado and San Diego, Arenado went 10-for-23 (.435) with three homers, two doubles and 5 RBIs.
With a two-run home run in San Diego on Friday, the 35-year-old notched his eighth 30-homer season and his first since 2022 with the Cardinals. The only players with more 30-homer seasons as primary third basemen are Hall of Famers Mike Schmidt (12) and Eddie Mathews (10).
Acuña has a complicated history with the loanDepot park outfield. This March, he clinched a World Baseball Classic championship there with Team Venezuela; but in July 2021, the right fielder tore his right ACL while leaping for a ball near the fence, sidelining him for the remainder of the Braves’ World Series campaign. On Saturday afternoon, less than 72 hours before kicking off a run at another title, Acuña proved he truly has no fear of the Miami warning track.
With no outs and a runner on first in the opening frame, Marlins slugger Heriberto Hernández lofted a Brent Suter sinker the opposite way at 101.2 mph. Acuña darted to his right at 25.6 feet per second, leapt at the fence and went tumbling to the dirt with the ball secured, giving the Braves a loud first out of the game. (Hernández went on to record his 25th homer the next day, wisely pulling the ball to left field rather than testing Acuña again.)

MILWAUKEE — Team captains are not common in Major League Baseball. But on Saturday, the Milwaukee Brewers named Christian Yelich the first captain in franchise history, making him one of only three active captains in the majors.
The Brewers decided in a team meeting prior to its Saturday game against the St. Louis Cardinals to give the honor to Yelich. But Yelich did not want to accept without “sign-off” from another Brewers legend: Robin Yount.
Yelich requested that Yount, who played his entire 20-year career with Milwaukee, sign off on his captaincy before accepting. Yount, a Hall of Famer, was a leader on the only Brewers’ team to make the World Series in 1982.
Yount joined Wisconsin’s Midday News to discuss the conversations he had with Yelich and Brewers Manager Pat Murphy ahead of Saturday’s announcement.
“In all honesty, they certainly didn’t need my approval,” Yount said. “But in saying that, it was very, very humbling to be honest, to think that they would even consider asking me what I thought.”
Yount said the fact that he was asked speaks to the character of this team, calling them a “class act, especially at this time of the season.”
While Yount has not been around the current Brewers team as much as in previous years, he said he got to know Yelich through their mutual friend, Bob Uecker.
“I learned a lot about Christian through the years Ueck was around him,” Yount said. “Ueck spoke of Christian in the highest regard… The team pretty much looked up to him as that guy. And that’s all I needed to hear from somebody that was around him enough.”
